The list of international presidential trips made by Donald Trump documents the overseas journeys conducted by the 45th and 47th President of the United States during his non-consecutive terms in office, from January 2017 to January 2021 and from January 2025 onward.[[1]](#ref-1)
These trips, totaling 19 multi-country itineraries to 22 distinct nations during the first term, marked a departure from the higher travel volume of prior administrations, aligning with an emphasis on targeted bilateral diplomacy, summitry on trade and security, and reduced multilateral engagements to focus resources domestically.[[1]](#ref-1) Notable among them was Trump's inaugural 2017 visit to Saudi Arabia, where he addressed Muslim leaders on counterterrorism and secured a $110 billion arms agreement, followed by stops in Israel— including a historic address at the Western Wall—and the Vatican for talks with Pope Francis on religious liberty.[[1]](#ref-1) Subsequent journeys encompassed North Korea summits in Singapore (2018) and Vietnam (2019) with Kim Jong-un to pursue denuclearization, G20 gatherings in Argentina and Japan addressing global trade imbalances, and unannounced visits to U.S. troops in war zones like Afghanistan.[[1]](#ref-1) Defining characteristics included a pragmatic focus on economic leverage—evident in renegotiated alliances pressuring NATO members to boost defense spending, which rose collectively by over $130 billion during his tenure—and avoidance of extended tours amid domestic priorities, though controversies arose from candid summit rhetoric, such as the 2018 Helsinki press conference with Vladimir Putin prioritizing dialogue over confrontation.[[1]](#ref-1) In the second term, as of October 2025, Trump has pursued a renewed itinerary with early Middle East engagements in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE to reinforce energy and security pacts, alongside a six-day Asia tour encompassing Malaysia for ASEAN discussions, Japan for alliance reaffirmations, and South Korea amid prospective talks with China's Xi Jinping on tariffs and technology transfers.[[2]](#ref-2)[[3]](#ref-3) These efforts underscore continuity in deal-oriented foreign policy, leveraging personal summits to extract concessions on trade deficits and regional stability.[[3]](#ref-3)

## Summary

### Aggregate statistics and patterns

During his first presidency (2017–2021), Donald Trump made 19 international trips, visiting 25 countries in addition to the West Bank.[[2]](#ref-2) These included multiple engagements in the Middle East, Europe, and Asia, with early emphasis on allies such as Saudi Arabia and Israel.[[1]](#ref-1) Trip frequency peaked in 2017 with several multi-country itineraries, including his inaugural foreign visit encompassing Saudi Arabia, Israel, the Palestinian Authority, the Vatican, Belgium, and Italy.[[4]](#ref-4)
Activity diminished progressively, culminating in zero international trips in 2020 due to restrictions imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic, which empirically curtailed global presidential travel.[[1]](#ref-1) This pattern reflects initial relationship-building followed by selective diplomacy amid domestic priorities and external constraints.
In his second presidency (2025–present), as of October 2025, Trump has conducted 8 international trips to 11 countries, with seven foreign countries visited in the first six months alone.[[5]](#ref-5) Renewed focus appears on the Middle East, including a May 2025 tour of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates, alongside an October Asia itinerary involving deal-making in Southeast Asia.[[2]](#ref-2) [[6]](#ref-6)
Across both terms, observable trends include repeated visits to select allies—such as the United Kingdom (five times total) and Japan (three times)—and a strategic orientation toward bilateral summits with both partners like European NATO members and adversaries including North Korea.[[7]](#ref-7) Regional distribution prioritizes the Middle East and Indo-Pacific over Latin America or Africa, aligning with causal priorities of security alliances and economic negotiations rather than universal engagement.[[8]](#ref-8)

### Differences between presidencies

Trump's first presidency saw international trips emphasizing the renegotiation of alliances under an "America First" doctrine, with a focus on urging NATO allies to increase defense spending to address burden-sharing imbalances and counter emerging threats from China's economic and military expansion.[[4]](#ref-4) This approach reflected a global environment of relative stability before the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, prioritizing bilateral deals to rectify perceived unfair trade practices and multilateral engagements like G7 and G20 summits. In his second term, trip planning has accelerated toward pragmatic deal-making in energy security and strategic partnerships, driven by Europe's post-Ukraine vulnerabilities to Russian gas supplies and intensified U.S. efforts to export liquefied natural gas while fortifying alliances against Sino-Russian coordination.[[9]](#ref-9)
Logistically, the first term's 19 trips across 2017–2019 were disrupted in 2020 by the COVID-19 pandemic, which imposed travel restrictions and limited presidential outings to essential domestic responses, resulting in minimal foreign engagements that year.[[1]](#ref-1) The second term, unencumbered by such health crises, has pursued a brisk early schedule—eight trips to 11 countries by October 2025—capitalizing on post-inauguration momentum to address urgent geopolitical shifts, including Asia-Pacific realignments amid tariff negotiations and supply chain decoupling from China.[[7]](#ref-7)
Accompaniment evolved from first-term inclusions of corporate executives to advance trade agendas, as seen in missions promoting U.S. business interests during summits, to a second-term emphasis on national security advisors and military liaisons, aligning with priorities like border fortifications and deterrence against adversarial powers.[[10]](#ref-10)[[11]](#ref-11) This shift mirrors causal changes in threat landscapes, where economic diplomacy yielded to integrated security-trade strategies post-Ukraine and amid verified escalations in Chinese assertiveness.[[12]](#ref-12)

## First presidency trips (2017–2021)

### 2017

President Donald Trump's international travel in 2017 commenced with a five-country itinerary from May 20 to May 27, emphasizing bilateral engagements in the Middle East and Europe to advance counterterrorism cooperation, economic partnerships, and alliance reassessments. The trip began in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on May 20–22, where Trump met King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Gulf Cooperation Council leaders, announcing a $110 billion arms sales agreement and a $350 billion 10-year defense commitment aimed at strengthening regional security against Iran and extremism.[[1]](#ref-1)
From Riyadh, Trump proceeded to Jerusalem, Israel, on May 22–23, meeting President Reuven Rivlin and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; he became the first sitting U.S. president to visit the Western Wall, signaling support for Israel's security and laying groundwork for Middle East peace initiatives focused on economic incentives over traditional frameworks.[[1]](#ref-1)
On May 23, in Bethlehem, West Bank, Trump held discussions with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, urging reforms to combat incitement and promote prosperity as prerequisites for negotiations.[[1]](#ref-1)
The itinerary continued to Vatican City on May 24 for a meeting with Pope Francis, discussing shared concerns on religious persecution and family values, followed by Brussels, Belgium, on May 24–25, where Trump conferred with NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg and pressed allies on defense spending burdens.[[1]](#ref-1)
Concluding in Taormina, Italy, on May 25–26, Trump engaged Italian President Sergio Mattarella and Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni on trade and migration, while critiquing multilateral trade imbalances during associated discussions.[[1]](#ref-1)
In July, Trump visited Warsaw, Poland, on July 6, meeting President Andrzej Duda and delivering a speech at Krasinski Square emphasizing Western civilization's defense against radical Islamic terrorism and sovereignty against external pressures.[[1]](#ref-1) The stop supported the Three Seas Initiative for Central European energy independence and preceded bilateral side meetings in Hamburg, Germany, on July 6–8, including a two-hour discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Syria, election interference allegations, and Ukraine.[[1]](#ref-1)
Trump's November Asia tour, spanning November 5–14, featured bilateral engagements to promote fair trade and counter North Korean threats. In Tokyo, Japan, on November 5–6, he met Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, announcing strengthened defense ties and $12.1 billion in business deals.[[1]](#ref-1)
In Seoul, South Korea, on November 7–8, discussions with President Moon Jae-in focused on alliance enhancements and pressure on Pyongyang.[[1]](#ref-1)
Beijing hosted Trump on November 8–10 for talks with President Xi Jinping, yielding $250 billion in trade agreements and pledges for North Korea sanctions enforcement.[[1]](#ref-1)
The tour extended to Da Nang and Hanoi, Vietnam, on November 10–12, for meetings with General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong on economic cooperation, and Manila, Philippines, on November 12–14, where President Rodrigo Duterte hosted discussions on counterterrorism and maritime security.[[1]](#ref-1) These stops utilized Air Force One for transcontinental logistics, with security protocols adapted to the nascent administration's operational tempo.[[13]](#ref-13)

### 2018

In 2018, President Trump conducted seven international trips, emphasizing trade negotiations amid the intensifying U.S.-China trade dispute, multilateral security commitments, and direct diplomacy with North Korea's leadership. These visits reflected a pattern of prioritizing bilateral leverage and "America First" economic agendas over broad multilateral consensus, including contentious G7 and G20 engagements where Trump advocated for reduced trade barriers and increased allied defense contributions. Outcomes included a temporary U.S.-China tariff truce but limited progress on North Korean denuclearization beyond symbolic gestures, with no resumption of International Atomic Energy Agency inspections.[[1]](#ref-1)[[14]](#ref-14)
The year's travels began with the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland (January 22–26), where Trump delivered a keynote promoting U.S. investment opportunities and criticizing unfair trade practices, positioning America as an economic powerhouse open to deals.[[1]](#ref-1) This was followed by no major trips until mid-year, aligning with domestic focus ahead of midterm elections.
In June, Trump attended the G7 Summit in Charlevoix, Canada (June 8–9), where discussions centered on trade imbalances; he departed early, withdrawing U.S. endorsement of the joint communique after public criticism of Canadian tariffs and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.[[1]](#ref-1)[[15]](#ref-15) Immediately transitioning, he held the first-ever U.S.-North Korea summit in Singapore (June 10–13) with Chairman Kim Jong-un, yielding a joint statement committing to "complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" and U.S. security guarantees, though lacking timelines or verification mechanisms.[[1]](#ref-1) Subsequent U.S. verifications included satellite and on-site observations of North Korea's partial dismantling of the Sohae satellite launch facility in July, but no comprehensive inspections occurred, and missile tests resumed later in the year.
Later trips included the NATO Summit in Brussels, Belgium (July 11–12), where Trump demanded allies meet 2% GDP defense spending targets, claiming post-summit increases in commitments totaling over $266 billion in additional allied spending.[[16]](#ref-16) A working visit to the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom) (July 13–15) involved meetings with [Prime Minister](/page/Prime_minister) [Theresa May](/page/Theresa_May) on post-Brexit trade prospects and Queen Elizabeth II at [Windsor Castle](/page/Windsor_Castle), amid discussions of defense [cooperation](/page/Cooperation) and [technology](/page/Technology) transfers, though overshadowed by domestic protests.[[17]](#ref-17)
In November, Trump traveled to Paris, France (November 9–11) for World War I Armistice centennial commemorations, meeting President Emmanuel Macron and honoring U.S. fallen at Suresnes American Cemetery, while tensions arose over Macron's warnings against nationalism.[[18]](#ref-18)[[19]](#ref-19) The year closed at the G20 Summit in Buenos Aires, Argentina (November 30–December 1), featuring a bilateral dinner with Xi Jinping yielding a 90-day freeze on new tariffs to allow negotiations, alongside meetings with host President Mauricio Macri on energy and trade; a planned Putin encounter was canceled following Russia's Ukraine port seizure.[[20]](#ref-20)[[14]](#ref-14)

These engagements demonstrated causal persistence in Trump's approach of using summit leverage to enforce U.S. interests, as evidenced by the Hanoi walkout preventing premature concessions and G20 trade pauses averting further escalation without yielding core demands like structural Chinese reforms. European visits recalibrated alliances by spotlighting historical U.S. contributions, countering narratives of isolationism while pressing for equitable contributions, though mainstream analyses often downplayed tangible diplomatic holds in favor of stylistic critiques.[[21]](#ref-21)

### 2020

In 2020, President Donald Trump's international travel was sharply curtailed following the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic, with only two foreign trips recorded before global restrictions intensified. The World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a public health emergency of international concern on January 30 and a pandemic on March 11, prompting widespread suspension of non-essential international engagements by world leaders, including Trump. This represented a significant empirical reduction from prior years, shifting focus to virtual diplomacy and domestic priorities amid rising U.S. case counts, which exceeded 1 million by April. Despite the abbreviated scope, the year's diplomacy yielded high-stakes outcomes, notably the Abraham Accords, which formalized normalization agreements between Israel and the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, signed at the White House on September 15 with visiting foreign leaders.

## Second presidency trips (2025–present)

### 2025

In May 2025, President Trump undertook his inaugural foreign trip of the second term, a four-day Middle East itinerary from May 13 to 16 focused on Gulf Cooperation Council engagements to advance energy security and investment commitments amid U.S. priorities for domestic energy production expansion.[[32]](#ref-32)[[33]](#ref-33) The route commenced in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, where Trump met King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to discuss oil output stabilization and secured a $600 billion investment commitment from Saudi Arabia into U.S. infrastructure and technology sectors, as part of reported prospective Gulf investments.[[34]](#ref-34)[[35]](#ref-35)[[36]](#ref-36) Proceedings extended to Doha, Qatar, for consultations at the Al Udeid Air Base—the largest U.S. military facility in the region—emphasizing enhanced basing agreements and counterterrorism cooperation, followed by Abu Dhabi and Dubai in the UAE for bilateral pacts on AI development and semiconductor supply chain diversification away from adversarial dependencies.[[37]](#ref-37)[[38]](#ref-38) Outcomes included non-binding memoranda for LNG exports to support U.S. energy independence goals, with Gulf states committing to reduced reliance on Chinese tech imports.[[32]](#ref-32)[[39]](#ref-39)

During the May 2025 tour of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates, the White House announced investment and economic commitments totaling over $2 trillion. Specific breakdowns included a $600 billion investment pledge from Saudi Arabia (later referenced as expanding toward $1 trillion), a $1.2 trillion "economic exchange" with Qatar (with signed deals listed at $243.5 billion, including major Boeing aircraft sales), and $200 billion in new commercial deals with the UAE building on a prior $1.4 trillion 10-year framework. Independent analyses, such as Reuters' tally of specific announced deals, estimated the verifiable total closer to $700–730 billion, noting many were non-binding memoranda of understanding (MoUs), multi-year frameworks, or projects already in progress before the tour. Fact-checks from outlets like BBC, AP, and The New York Times highlighted similar patterns of inflated headline numbers for political optics, echoing Trump's 2017 Saudi Arabia visit where $450 billion in deals were announced but actual tracked trade and investment flows amounted to less than $300 billion between 2017 and 2020.
The combined annual GDP of Saudi Arabia ($1.1 trillion), UAE ($550 billion), and Qatar (~$220 billion) totals approximately $2–2.3 trillion (2025–2026 estimates), underscoring the implausibility of immediate $6 trillion transfers or short-term commitments without significant economic disruption. These announcements aimed to boost U.S. manufacturing, technology, defense, and energy sectors while countering Chinese influence, though long-term realization depends on implementation, oil prices, and geopolitics.
Trump's subsequent international engagement in 2025, as of October 26, involved an ongoing Asia-Pacific tour commencing October 24, spanning Malaysia, Japan, and South Korea to address trade imbalances and coordinate on China containment strategies.[[12]](#ref-12)[[6]](#ref-6) The itinerary opened in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, for the ASEAN Summit on October 26–28, where Trump pursued multilateral frameworks for supply chain resilience and tariff alignments against Chinese overproduction in electronics and rare earths.[[41]](#ref-41)[[42]](#ref-42) Subsequent stops included Tokyo, Japan, for talks with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on defense burden-sharing and currency manipulation curbs, followed by Seoul, South Korea, encompassing a planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate phased tariff reductions tied to intellectual property enforcement and market access concessions.[[43]](#ref-43)[[44]](#ref-44) Objectives centered on bilateral trade recalibrations to favor U.S. manufacturing revival, with preliminary discussions yielding commitments for Japanese and South Korean investments in American semiconductor facilities.[[11]](#ref-11)[[45]](#ref-45)

## Multilateral engagements

### First presidency

During his first presidency (2017–2021), Donald Trump participated in key multilateral forums including NATO summits, G7 and G20 meetings, and United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) sessions, advancing an "America First" approach that prioritized U.S. economic interests, national sovereignty, and equitable burden-sharing among allies.[[4]](#ref-4)[[47]](#ref-47) This stance often diverged from consensus-driven outcomes, as Trump critiqued arrangements perceived to impose asymmetric costs on the U.S., such as defense contributions in NATO or climate commitments in G7/G20 declarations lacking reciprocal obligations from major emitters like China.[[48]](#ref-48) Empirical data from these engagements showed tangible shifts, including accelerated NATO ally defense expenditures following U.S. pressure for 2% GDP targets, rising from an average of 1.47% in 2016 to 1.72% by 2020, with the number of compliant allies doubling to 10.[[49]](#ref-49)
![G7 Taormina family photo 2017-05-26.jpg][float-right]
At NATO summits—in Brussels (2017 and 2018) and London (2019)—Trump repeatedly highlighted insufficient European burden-sharing, asserting that the U.S. shouldered disproportionate costs relative to threats faced, and linking alliance credibility to meeting the 2% GDP defense spending guideline established in 2014 but unevenly pursued.[[50]](#ref-50) His direct critiques, including warnings of potential U.S. withdrawal from collective defense obligations absent reforms, correlated with subsequent pledges and actual increases: non-U.S. allies boosted expenditures by approximately $130 billion cumulatively from 2016 to 2020, with commitments at the 2018 summit explicitly crediting U.S. advocacy for renewed momentum.[[51]](#ref-51) This pressure yielded verifiable outcomes, as six additional European allies met or exceeded the 2% threshold by 2020 compared to pre-2017 levels, enhancing alliance capabilities amid Russian aggression in Ukraine and elsewhere.[[52]](#ref-52)
In G7 summits (Taormina, Italy, 2017; Charlevoix, Canada, 2018; Biarritz, France, 2019) and G20 gatherings (Hamburg, Germany, 2017; Buenos Aires, Argentina, 2018; Osaka, Japan, 2019), Trump advocated for trade reciprocity and rejected blanket endorsements of multilateral climate pacts, arguing they disadvantaged U.S. workers through unverified economic models and unequal burdens—China's emissions exemptions, for instance, allowed it to increase coal reliance while U.S. manufacturing faced deindustrialization risks.[[53]](#ref-53) At the 2017 G7, he declined to reaffirm Paris Agreement commitments, citing cost-benefit analyses showing annual U.S. compliance burdens exceeding $3 trillion in lost GDP by 2040 without commensurate global reductions.[[54]](#ref-54) G20 discussions emphasized fairer global economic load-sharing, with Trump blocking subsidies for inefficient state-owned enterprises and pushing for tariff eliminations, though tensions arose over U.S. steel tariffs; outcomes included side agreements on digital trade and energy access, reflecting partial alignment on market-driven principles over regulatory harmonization.[[55]](#ref-55)
Trump's annual UNGA addresses (2017–2019) underscored sovereignty as the bedrock of peace, rejecting supranational overreach and naming threats from Iran (its nuclear ambitions and regional proxy support), North Korea ("rocket man" regime's missile tests), and China (South China Sea militarization and unfair trade practices eroding U.S. sovereignty).[[56]](#ref-56)[[48]](#ref-48) In 2018, he declared sovereign nations the sole guarantors of freedom, criticizing globalist ideologies and Iran's "hypocritical" regime for exporting instability while facing domestic protests.[[57]](#ref-57) The 2019 speech extended warnings to China's predatory lending and intellectual property theft, framing multilateralism as effective only when nations upheld borders and self-determination rather than ceding authority to unelected bodies.[[58]](#ref-58) These interventions, while isolating the U.S. from some resolutions, aligned with causal realism by conditioning cooperation on verifiable reciprocity, influencing downstream shifts like heightened UN scrutiny of Iranian sanctions evasion.[[59]](#ref-59)

### Second presidency

During his second presidency, Donald Trump participated in select multilateral forums, emphasizing bilateral-style negotiations within group settings to advance U.S. economic and security interests, particularly in countering Chinese influence and addressing supply chain dependencies on rare earths and critical minerals.[[60]](#ref-60)[[61]](#ref-61) This approach reflected a continuation of transactional diplomacy, prioritizing verifiable deals over broad institutional commitments, amid executive actions imposing tariffs on imports and promoting U.S. energy exports to allies.[[11]](#ref-11)[[6]](#ref-6)
Trump attended the 51st G7 Summit in Kananaskis, Alberta, Canada, on June 16–17, 2025, where discussions centered on global economic stability, Ukraine policy, and trade imbalances. He advocated a firm stance on Russia, linking aid to territorial concessions, while pushing for reduced reliance on adversarial supply chains through tariff measures and allied energy diversification. Trump departed the summit early to focus on domestic priorities, signaling limited enthusiasm for prolonged multilateral deliberations.[[62]](#ref-62)[[63]](#ref-63)
In October 2025, Trump traveled to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, for the 47th ASEAN Summit on October 26, marking the first U.S. presidential attendance since 2022. Amid regional concerns over Chinese assertiveness in the South China Sea and trade disruptions, he facilitated a ceasefire agreement between Cambodia and Thailand, witnessed its signing, and concluded trade pacts with Malaysia, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam to secure access to rare earth minerals and bolster U.S. exports. These outcomes underscored a shift toward de-risking global supply chains via targeted deals rather than expansive regional frameworks, with Trump highlighting potential face-to-face talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping later in the Asia tour to enforce tariff compliance.[[64]](#ref-64)[[65]](#ref-65)[[46]](#ref-46)[[61]](#ref-61)
Trump declined to attend the 2025 G20 Summit in Johannesburg, South Africa, delegating Vice President JD Vance, consistent with a strategy favoring high-yield engagements over routine global assemblies. No verified participation in UN General Assembly or APEC events occurred by late October 2025, aligning with broader withdrawals from multilateral bodies like the WHO and Paris Agreement to redirect resources toward bilateral leverage.[[66]](#ref-66)[[67]](#ref-67)

## Diplomatic outcomes and evaluations

### Verifiable achievements and causal impacts

During President Trump's first foreign trip to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on May 20, 2017, the United States and Saudi Arabia finalized letters of intent for arms sales valued at $110 billion, including tanks, missile systems, and aircraft, with frameworks for up to $350 billion in defense cooperation over the subsequent decade; these agreements bolstered Saudi defensive capabilities against regional threats, with deliveries commencing in 2018.[[68]](#ref-68)[[69]](#ref-69)
At the G20 summit in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on November 30, 2018, Trump signed the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), modernizing NAFTA by strengthening labor provisions, digital trade rules, and intellectual property protections; implementation in 2020 correlated with a 15% increase in U.S. exports to Mexico in high-wage manufacturing sectors by 2022.[[70]](#ref-70)
Trump's attendance at the G20 summit in Osaka, Japan, on June 28-29, 2019, facilitated bilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping that advanced negotiations culminating in the Phase One U.S.-China Economic and Trade Agreement signed on January 15, 2020; under the deal, China committed to purchasing $200 billion in additional U.S. goods and services over two years, including $77 billion in manufactured products, yielding $123 billion in verified U.S. agricultural exports to China in 2020-2021.[[71]](#ref-71)
Trump's participation in NATO summits, including Warsaw in July 2017 and Brussels in July 2018, featured explicit calls for burden-sharing, contributing to a rise in alliance-wide defense spending from 1.42% of collective GDP in 2016 to 1.84% in 2020, with ten members achieving the 2% target by 2020 compared to three previously; econometric analyses attribute approximately 0.2-0.3 percentage points of the increase directly to U.S. pressure exerted during these engagements.[[72]](#ref-72)
In May 2025, Trump's tour of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates secured a $600 billion investment pledge from Saudi Arabia in U.S. energy, technology, and infrastructure projects, alongside over $2 trillion in total Gulf commitments for American exports and joint ventures, enhancing supply chain diversification away from China-dependent sources.[[36]](#ref-36)[[73]](#ref-73)
During the October 2025 Asia trip, Trump signed reciprocal trade agreements with Malaysia and Cambodia, opening markets for $50 billion in annual U.S. agricultural and manufacturing exports while imposing tariffs on non-reciprocal partners, and obtained a $550 billion investment commitment from Japan focused on semiconductors and critical minerals to reduce reliance on Chinese supply chains.[[74]](#ref-74)[[75]](#ref-75)

### Criticisms, controversies, and counter-narratives

Trump's engagements at NATO summits, particularly in 2018 and beyond, drew criticism from European leaders and U.S. media outlets for his public demands that allies increase defense spending to 2% of GDP, often framed as a "shakedown" or extortionate diplomacy that undermined alliance cohesion.[[76]](#ref-76)[[77]](#ref-77) However, empirical data shows NATO members meeting the 2% threshold rose from six in 2016 to 23 by 2025, with subsequent commitments to a 5% target by 2035 explicitly linked to sustained pressure from Trump-era policies, suggesting causal effectiveness in burden-sharing despite initial diplomatic friction.[[78]](#ref-78)[[79]](#ref-79)
The 2017 Saudi Arabia visit provoked media mockery over Trump's participation in a traditional sword dance, portrayed in outlets like The Guardian and Vanity Fair as awkward subservience or cultural insensitivity, with little contemporaneous emphasis on the $110 billion arms deal signed during the trip, which bolstered U.S. defense exports and Saudi commitments against Iran.[[80]](#ref-80)[[81]](#ref-81)[[82]](#ref-82) Counter-narratives from defense analysts highlight that such optics critiques often overlooked the deal's strategic value, including immediate sales of tanks and missile systems, amid a pattern of left-leaning media prioritizing stylistic gaffes over transactional outcomes verifiable in export records.[[83]](#ref-83)
Summits with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in 2018 and 2019 faced accusations of failure from critics, including Brookings Institution reports citing the Hanoi walkout and lack of verifiable denuclearization, yet North Korea conducted no intercontinental ballistic missile tests or nuclear detonations between November 2017 and post-presidency resumption in 2022, a de facto pause attributed by Trump supporters to personal diplomacy's deterrent effect.[[84]](#ref-84)[[85]](#ref-85) While short-range tests persisted, challenging full success claims, the absence of escalatory long-range activity during engagement contrasts with pre-2018 acceleration, underscoring debates over whether summits achieved temporary stabilization absent from prior sanctions-only approaches.[[86]](#ref-86)
In Trump's second term, 2025 trips to Asia and the Gulf elicited protests and warnings of economic risks from outlets like Politico, framing deal-focused itineraries as reckless amid trade tensions, yet parallels to first-term successes—such as Saudi investments—suggest media amplification of potential downsides over historical precedents of U.S. leverage gains.[[11]](#ref-11) Isolationist voices on the right critiqued excessive multilateralism, while globalist left-leaning perspectives decried transactionalism as eroding norms, but causal assessments indicate net benefits like heightened allied contributions and restrained adversaries, unmarred by the systemic biases in coverage that downplay empirical metrics for narrative-driven alarmism.[[87]](#ref-87)[[88]](#ref-88)

The list of international presidential trips made by Donald Trump documents the overseas journeys conducted by the 45th and 47th President of the United States during his non-consecutive terms in office, from January 2017 to January 2021 and from January 2025 onward.[[1]](#ref-1)
These trips, totaling 19 multi-country itineraries to 22 distinct nations during the first term, marked a departure from the higher travel volume of prior administrations, aligning with an emphasis on targeted bilateral diplomacy, summitry on trade and security, and reduced multilateral engagements to focus resources domestically.[[1]](#ref-1) Notable among them was Trump's inaugural 2017 visit to Saudi Arabia, where he addressed Muslim leaders on counterterrorism and secured a $110 billion arms agreement, followed by stops in Israel— including a historic address at the Western Wall—and the Vatican for talks with Pope Francis on religious liberty.[[1]](#ref-1) Subsequent journeys encompassed North Korea summits in Singapore (2018) and Vietnam (2019) with Kim Jong-un to pursue denuclearization, G20 gatherings in Argentina and Japan addressing global trade imbalances, and unannounced visits to U.S. troops in war zones like Afghanistan.[[1]](#ref-1) Defining characteristics included a pragmatic focus on economic leverage—evident in renegotiated alliances pressuring NATO members to boost defense spending, which rose collectively by over $130 billion during his tenure—and avoidance of extended tours amid domestic priorities, though controversies arose from candid summit rhetoric, such as the 2018 Helsinki press conference with Vladimir Putin prioritizing dialogue over confrontation.[[1]](#ref-1) In the second term, as of October 2025, Trump has pursued a renewed itinerary with early Middle East engagements in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE to reinforce energy and security pacts, alongside a six-day Asia tour encompassing Malaysia for ASEAN discussions, Japan for alliance reaffirmations, and South Korea amid prospective talks with China's Xi Jinping on tariffs and technology transfers.[[2]](#ref-2)[[3]](#ref-3) These efforts underscore continuity in deal-oriented foreign policy, leveraging personal summits to extract concessions on trade deficits and regional stability.[[3]](#ref-3)

## Summary

### Aggregate statistics and patterns

During his first presidency (2017–2021), Donald Trump made 19 international trips, visiting 25 countries in addition to the West Bank.[[2]](#ref-2) These included multiple engagements in the Middle East, Europe, and Asia, with early emphasis on allies such as Saudi Arabia and Israel.[[1]](#ref-1) Trip frequency peaked in 2017 with several multi-country itineraries, including his inaugural foreign visit encompassing Saudi Arabia, Israel, the Palestinian Authority, the Vatican, Belgium, and Italy.[[4]](#ref-4)
Activity diminished progressively, culminating in zero international trips in 2020 due to restrictions imposed by the COVID-19 pandemic, which empirically curtailed global presidential travel.[[1]](#ref-1) This pattern reflects initial relationship-building followed by selective diplomacy amid domestic priorities and external constraints.
In his second presidency (2025–present), as of October 2025, Trump has conducted 8 international trips to 11 countries, with seven foreign countries visited in the first six months alone.[[5]](#ref-5) Renewed focus appears on the Middle East, including a May 2025 tour of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates, alongside an October Asia itinerary involving deal-making in Southeast Asia.[[2]](#ref-2) [[6]](#ref-6)
Across both terms, observable trends include repeated visits to select allies—such as the United Kingdom (five times total) and Japan (three times)—and a strategic orientation toward bilateral summits with both partners like European NATO members and adversaries including North Korea.[[7]](#ref-7) Regional distribution prioritizes the Middle East and Indo-Pacific over Latin America or Africa, aligning with causal priorities of security alliances and economic negotiations rather than universal engagement.[[8]](#ref-8)

### Differences between presidencies

Trump's first presidency saw international trips emphasizing the renegotiation of alliances under an "America First" doctrine, with a focus on urging NATO allies to increase defense spending to address burden-sharing imbalances and counter emerging threats from China's economic and military expansion.[[4]](#ref-4) This approach reflected a global environment of relative stability before the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, prioritizing bilateral deals to rectify perceived unfair trade practices and multilateral engagements like G7 and G20 summits. In his second term, trip planning has accelerated toward pragmatic deal-making in energy security and strategic partnerships, driven by Europe's post-Ukraine vulnerabilities to Russian gas supplies and intensified U.S. efforts to export liquefied natural gas while fortifying alliances against Sino-Russian coordination.[[9]](#ref-9)
Logistically, the first term's 19 trips across 2017–2019 were disrupted in 2020 by the COVID-19 pandemic, which imposed travel restrictions and limited presidential outings to essential domestic responses, resulting in minimal foreign engagements that year.[[1]](#ref-1) The second term, unencumbered by such health crises, has pursued a brisk early schedule—eight trips to 11 countries by October 2025—capitalizing on post-inauguration momentum to address urgent geopolitical shifts, including Asia-Pacific realignments amid tariff negotiations and supply chain decoupling from China.[[7]](#ref-7)
Accompaniment evolved from first-term inclusions of corporate executives to advance trade agendas, as seen in missions promoting U.S. business interests during summits, to a second-term emphasis on national security advisors and military liaisons, aligning with priorities like border fortifications and deterrence against adversarial powers.[[10]](#ref-10)[[11]](#ref-11) This shift mirrors causal changes in threat landscapes, where economic diplomacy yielded to integrated security-trade strategies post-Ukraine and amid verified escalations in Chinese assertiveness.[[12]](#ref-12)

## First presidency trips (2017–2021)

### 2017

President Donald Trump's international travel in 2017 commenced with a five-country itinerary from May 20 to May 27, emphasizing bilateral engagements in the Middle East and Europe to advance counterterrorism cooperation, economic partnerships, and alliance reassessments. The trip began in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on May 20–22, where Trump met King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Gulf Cooperation Council leaders, announcing a $110 billion arms sales agreement and a $350 billion 10-year defense commitment aimed at strengthening regional security against Iran and extremism.[[1]](#ref-1)
From Riyadh, Trump proceeded to Jerusalem, Israel, on May 22–23, meeting President Reuven Rivlin and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; he became the first sitting U.S. president to visit the Western Wall, signaling support for Israel's security and laying groundwork for Middle East peace initiatives focused on economic incentives over traditional frameworks.[[1]](#ref-1)
On May 23, in Bethlehem, West Bank, Trump held discussions with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, urging reforms to combat incitement and promote prosperity as prerequisites for negotiations.[[1]](#ref-1)
The itinerary continued to Vatican City on May 24 for a meeting with Pope Francis, discussing shared concerns on religious persecution and family values, followed by Brussels, Belgium, on May 24–25, where Trump conferred with NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg and pressed allies on defense spending burdens.[[1]](#ref-1)
Concluding in Taormina, Italy, on May 25–26, Trump engaged Italian President Sergio Mattarella and Prime Minister Paolo Gentiloni on trade and migration, while critiquing multilateral trade imbalances during associated discussions.[[1]](#ref-1)
In July, Trump visited Warsaw, Poland, on July 6, meeting President Andrzej Duda and delivering a speech at Krasinski Square emphasizing Western civilization's defense against radical Islamic terrorism and sovereignty against external pressures.[[1]](#ref-1) The stop supported the Three Seas Initiative for Central European energy independence and preceded bilateral side meetings in Hamburg, Germany, on July 6–8, including a two-hour discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Syria, election interference allegations, and Ukraine.[[1]](#ref-1)
Trump's November Asia tour, spanning November 5–14, featured bilateral engagements to promote fair trade and counter North Korean threats. In Tokyo, Japan, on November 5–6, he met Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, announcing strengthened defense ties and $12.1 billion in business deals.[[1]](#ref-1)
In Seoul, South Korea, on November 7–8, discussions with President Moon Jae-in focused on alliance enhancements and pressure on Pyongyang.[[1]](#ref-1)
Beijing hosted Trump on November 8–10 for talks with President Xi Jinping, yielding $250 billion in trade agreements and pledges for North Korea sanctions enforcement.[[1]](#ref-1)
The tour extended to Da Nang and Hanoi, Vietnam, on November 10–12, for meetings with General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong on economic cooperation, and Manila, Philippines, on November 12–14, where President Rodrigo Duterte hosted discussions on counterterrorism and maritime security.[[1]](#ref-1) These stops utilized Air Force One for transcontinental logistics, with security protocols adapted to the nascent administration's operational tempo.[[13]](#ref-13)

### 2018

In 2018, President Trump conducted seven international trips, emphasizing trade negotiations amid the intensifying U.S.-China trade dispute, multilateral security commitments, and direct diplomacy with North Korea's leadership. These visits reflected a pattern of prioritizing bilateral leverage and "America First" economic agendas over broad multilateral consensus, including contentious G7 and G20 engagements where Trump advocated for reduced trade barriers and increased allied defense contributions. Outcomes included a temporary U.S.-China tariff truce but limited progress on North Korean denuclearization beyond symbolic gestures, with no resumption of International Atomic Energy Agency inspections.[[1]](#ref-1)[[14]](#ref-14)
The year's travels began with the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland (January 22–26), where Trump delivered a keynote promoting U.S. investment opportunities and criticizing unfair trade practices, positioning America as an economic powerhouse open to deals.[[1]](#ref-1) This was followed by no major trips until mid-year, aligning with domestic focus ahead of midterm elections.
In June, Trump attended the G7 Summit in Charlevoix, Canada (June 8–9), where discussions centered on trade imbalances; he departed early, withdrawing U.S. endorsement of the joint communique after public criticism of Canadian tariffs and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.[[1]](#ref-1)[[15]](#ref-15) Immediately transitioning, he held the first-ever U.S.-North Korea summit in Singapore (June 10–13) with Chairman Kim Jong-un, yielding a joint statement committing to "complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" and U.S. security guarantees, though lacking timelines or verification mechanisms.[[1]](#ref-1) Subsequent U.S. verifications included satellite and on-site observations of North Korea's partial dismantling of the Sohae satellite launch facility in July, but no comprehensive inspections occurred, and missile tests resumed later in the year.

### First presidency

During his first presidency (2017–2021), Donald Trump participated in key multilateral forums including NATO summits, G7 and G20 meetings, and United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) sessions, advancing an "America First" approach that prioritized U.S. economic interests, national sovereignty, and equitable burden-sharing among allies.[[4]](#ref-4)[[47]](#ref-47) This stance often diverged from consensus-driven outcomes, as Trump critiqued arrangements perceived to impose asymmetric costs on the U.S., such as defense contributions in NATO or climate commitments in G7/G20 declarations lacking reciprocal obligations from major emitters like China.[[48]](#ref-48) Empirical data from these engagements showed tangible shifts, including accelerated NATO ally defense expenditures following U.S. pressure for 2% GDP targets, rising from an average of 1.47% in 2016 to 1.72% by 2020, with the number of compliant allies doubling to 10.[[49]](#ref-49)

### Verifiable achievements and causal impacts

EXPLAINER
For the second time in his presidency, Donald Trump’s first official state visit is to Saudi Arabia.

For the second time in his presidency, Donald Trump has chosen Saudi Arabia as the destination for his first official state visit, following brief stops in Italy and the Vatican for Pope Francis’s funeral.
Trump [arrived](/news/liveblog/2025/5/13/live-us-president-donald-trump-embarks-on-historic-middle-east-trip) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on Tuesday just before 10am local time (07:00 GMT), where he was greeted by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The US president will [visit](/news/2025/5/12/trump-visits-saudi-arabia-qatar-uae-what-to-know) Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) from May 13 to 16, 2025.

## Which countries did Trump visit in his first term?
Trump visited 25 countries during his first term as the US president from January 2017 to January 2021.
The countries that Trump visited most during his first term include:

- France – Four times

- Japan, United Kingdom – Three times

- Belgium, Germany, Ireland, Italy, South Korea, Switzerland, Vietnam – Two times

- Afghanistan, Argentina, Canada, China, Finland, India, Iraq, Israel, North Korea, Palestine, Philippines, Poland, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Vatican City – Once

The order of his trips is listed in the infographic below.

Trump became the first US president to make the Middle East his first foreign destination, visiting Saudi Arabia on May 20-21, 2017.
He held bilateral talks with Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz and then-Deputy Crown Prince and Defence Minister Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) as the two countries signed a $110bn arms deal.
Trump also took part in the Riyadh Summit, a gathering of leaders from more than 50 Muslim-majority nations.
(Front R-L) Jordan’s King Abdullah II, Saudi Arabia’s King Salman bin Abdul Aziz Al Saud, US President Donald Trump, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim Bin Hamad Al Thani pose for a photo during Riyadh Summit, Saudi Arabia, May 21, 2017 [Jonathan Ernst/Reuters]After visiting Saudi Arabia, Trump travelled to Israel, where he met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and became the first sitting US president to visit the Western Wall in Jerusalem. He then met Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in the occupied West Bank city of Bethlehem.
Trump’s visit to India on February 24-25, 2020, was his final international trip before the COVID-19 pandemic led to global travel restrictions.

## The first country visited by each US president
A US president’s first trip is often seen as a signal of their priorities and foreign policy direction, setting the tone for how the US will engage with the world over the next four years.
In 1906, Theodore Roosevelt became the first sitting US president to travel abroad when he visited Panama to inspect the construction of the Panama Canal, a key project for US trade and military strategy.
More recently, in 1993, Bill Clinton’s first trip was to Canada, setting the stage for [NAFTA](/economy/2025/2/14/trumps-tariffs-could-spur-push-to-rewrite-north-america-trade-pact). In 2001, George W Bush visited Mexico, focusing on trade and immigration. Barack Obama’s first trip in 2009 was also to Canada, emphasising multilateral diplomacy. Joe Biden’s first trip in 2021 was to the UK, where he attended the G7 Summit, highlighting traditional alliances and climate change.

The international presidential trips made by [Joe Biden](/page/Joe_Biden) comprise his 36 official foreign visits as the 46th [President of the United States](/page/President_of_the_United_States), spanning January 20, 2021, to January 20, 2025, to 27 countries across [Europe](/page/Europe), [Asia](/page/Asia), the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East), [Africa](/page/Africa), and the [Americas](/page/Americas).[[1]](#ref-1) These travels emphasized multilateral diplomacy, including attendance at seven [G7](/page/G7) summits, five [G20](/page/G20) summits, and five [NATO](/page/NATO) summits, alongside bilateral engagements to coordinate responses to Russia's 2022 invasion of [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) and strategic competition with [China](/page/China) in the [Indo-Pacific](/page/Indo-Pacific).[[1]](#ref-1)
Biden's itinerary reflected a pattern of frequent European visits—13 in total—to reinforce NATO cohesion and deliver security assistance commitments, such as during his historic wartime trip to [Kyiv](/page/Kyiv) in February 2023, the first by a sitting U.S. president since the early [2000s](/page/2000s).[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2) In [Asia](/page/Asia), nine trips advanced partnerships through forums like the Quad and U.S.-[ASEAN](/page/ASEAN) summits, including state visits to [Japan](/page/Japan), [South Korea](/page/South_Korea), and [Vietnam](/page/Vietnam) to elevate economic and defense ties.[[1]](#ref-1) Later journeys marked precedents, such as the first presidential visits to [Angola](/page/Angola) in December 2024 and delayed engagements in [South America](/page/South_America) ([Peru](/page/Peru) and [Brazil](/page/Brazil) in November 2024), amid criticisms of delayed focus on regions like [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) and sub-[Saharan Africa](/page/Sub-Saharan_Africa) relative to predecessors.[[1]](#ref-1)[[3]](#ref-3) Early travel was constrained by the [COVID-19 pandemic](/page/COVID-19_pandemic), resulting in only six international trips in 2021—all to [Europe](/page/Europe)—compared to higher volumes by prior administrations in their initial years, before accelerating to 12 in 2022.[[4]](#ref-4) Defining elements included climate-focused attendance at COP26 and regional security consultations, such as in the Gulf and with Nordic leaders, though outcomes faced scrutiny over alliance strains and limited tangible concessions from adversaries like [Russia](/page/Russia) and [China](/page/China).[[1]](#ref-1)

## Summary

### Total Trips and Destinations

President Joe Biden conducted 21 international trips during his term, visiting 28 [countries](/page/List_of_companies_and_cities_in_Africa_that_manufacture_cement) in total, as documented in official records of presidential travels.[[1]](#ref-1) These engagements spanned [Europe](/page/Europe) (12 [countries](/page/List_of_companies_and_cities_in_Africa_that_manufacture_cement), including multiple returns to the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom), [Germany](/page/Germany), and [Poland](/page/Poland)), [Asia](/page/Asia) (9 [countries](/page/List_of_companies_and_cities_in_Africa_that_manufacture_cement), such as [Japan](/page/Japan), [India](/page/India), and [Vietnam](/page/Vietnam)), the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East) ([Israel](/page/Israel), [Saudi Arabia](/page/Saudi_Arabia), and the [West Bank](/page/West_Bank)), [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) ([Mexico](/page/Mexico), [Peru](/page/Peru), and [Brazil](/page/Brazil)), and [Africa](/page/Africa) ([Angola](/page/Angola) and [Cape Verde](/page/Cape_Verde)). The distribution emphasized [Europe](/page/Europe), accounting for the majority of destinations, with lighter representation from [Africa](/page/Africa) and [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) until the final year of his presidency.
Biden's travel included first-ever presidential visits to [Angola](/page/Angola) and [Cape Verde](/page/Cape_Verde) in December 2024, the latter part of a single African itinerary focused on sub-Saharan engagement after previous postponements of similar plans.[[5]](#ref-5)[[2]](#ref-2) Other delays affected destinations like an earlier [Angola](/page/Angola) trip and a [Germany](/page/Germany) visit, which occurred in October 2024.[[6]](#ref-6)
In comparison to predecessors, Biden's early-term pace—two trips in 2021, primarily to [Europe](/page/Europe)—was more restrained than Barack Obama's 13 trips in his first year or George W. Bush's 10, reflecting initial priorities on domestic [pandemic](/page/Pandemic) recovery and limited global mobility.[[7]](#ref-7) By contrast, [Donald](/page/Donald) Trump's first-year total reached 5 trips. Travel accelerated in 2022 with 7 itineraries across [Europe](/page/Europe), [Asia](/page/Asia), and the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East), aligning closer to historical norms for second-year engagements.[[4]](#ref-4)

### Primary Objectives and Patterns

The primary objectives of Joe Biden's international trips, as articulated in [White House](/page/White_House) statements, centered on restoring U.S. leadership among democracies, coordinating with [NATO](/page/NATO) allies on security challenges, and countering strategic competitors like [China](/page/China) through Indo-Pacific partnerships.[[8]](#ref-8)[[9]](#ref-9) Early rationales emphasized multilateral alliance reinforcement to address post-Afghanistan credibility concerns and global issues such as climate cooperation, reflecting a causal priority on rebuilding transatlantic unity amid perceived prior [isolationism](/page/Isolationism).[[10]](#ref-10)
Geopolitical patterns reveal a pronounced clustering of trips in [Europe](/page/Europe), driven by reactive responses to Russian threats, including the 2022 Ukraine invasion, which necessitated repeated [NATO](/page/NATO) and bilateral ally consultations for deterrence and support coordination.[[4]](#ref-4) This [Europe](/page/Europe)-centric focus—accounting for eight visits—contrasted with sparser [Asia](/page/Asia) engagements aimed at [China](/page/China) containment via alliances like the Quad, underscoring causal drivers of crisis proximity over balanced global outreach.[[6]](#ref-6) Travel frequency peaked early in the term with six international trips in 2021, declining markedly in 2024 to seven amid domestic election demands, a pattern attributable to resource allocation toward U.S. political imperatives rather than sustained foreign [diplomacy](/page/Diplomacy).[[4]](#ref-4)[[2]](#ref-2)
Over time, trip rationales shifted from broad multilateral resets in 2021—such as [G7](/page/G7) and [NATO](/page/NATO) summits—to more granular bilateral pledges, particularly for [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) aid and targeted [Asia](/page/Asia) diplomacy against [China](/page/China) expansionism, evidencing an evolution from foundational alliance repair to operational crisis management.[[11]](#ref-11) Logistically, these engagements relied on [Air Force One](/page/Air_Force_One) for secure transit, with per-hour operational costs exceeding $177,000, amplifying the fiscal stakes of such patterned deployments.[[12]](#ref-12) This progression highlights underlying causal realism: initial proactive multilateralism yielded to reactive [bilateralism](/page/Bilateralism) as acute threats like Russian aggression demanded direct, alliance-specific interventions over generalized forums.[[13]](#ref-13)

## Multilateral Engagements

### Major Summits Attended

President Biden attended the [G7](/page/G7) summits annually from 2021 to 2024, hosted respectively in [Carbis Bay](/page/Carbis_Bay), [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom) (June 11–13, 2021); [Schloss Elmau](/page/Schloss_Elmau), [Germany](/page/Germany) (June 26–28, 2022); [Hiroshima](/page/Hiroshima), [Japan](/page/Japan) (May 19–21, 2023); and [Borgo Egnazia](/page/Borgo_Egnazia), [Apulia](/page/Apulia), [Italy](/page/Italy) (June 13–15, 2024). These gatherings addressed economic resilience, global health security, and geopolitical tensions, with the [United States](/page/United_States) advocating for coordinated responses to [supply chain](/page/Supply_chain) disruptions and [energy security](/page/Energy_security). At the 2021 summit, Biden emphasized re-engagement with allies, committing $2 billion to the [COVAX](/page/COVAX) vaccine initiative and supporting a global infrastructure partnership to counter China's [Belt and Road Initiative](/page/Belt_and_Road_Initiative). In 2022, amid Russia's invasion of [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine), the U.S. position centered on food and [energy crisis](/page/Energy_crisis) mitigation, announcing $4.3 billion in global food aid pledges. The 2023 [Hiroshima](/page/Hiroshima) summit produced a vision statement on nuclear risks and free navigation in the [Indo-Pacific](/page/Indo-Pacific), with Biden pushing for de-risking from [China](/page/China) in critical technologies. The 2024 Apulia meeting focused on African partnerships and migration, where the U.S. highlighted private-sector investments in development to address root causes of instability.
For G20 summits, Biden participated in the 2022 Bali meeting (November 15–16, Indonesia), the 2023 New Delhi summit (September 9–10, India), and the 2024 Rio de Janeiro gathering (November 18–19, Brazil). Agendas emphasized sustainable development and multilateral reforms, with U.S. priorities including debt relief for low-income countries and climate finance mobilization. In Bali, despite tensions with host Indonesia's neutral stance on Ukraine, Biden secured consensus language condemning the invasion and advanced anti-corruption initiatives through a U.S.-led accountability framework. The New Delhi summit saw U.S. advocacy for inclusive growth, yielding commitments to tripling renewable energy capacity by 2030, though divisions persisted on Ukraine references. At Rio, the U.S. supported global alliance for people and planet, focusing on hunger reduction and digital economy standards.
Biden joined four NATO summits: [Brussels](/page/Brussels) (June 14, 2021), [Madrid](/page/Madrid) (June 28–30, 2022), [Vilnius](/page/Vilnius) (July 11–12, 2023), and [Washington, D.C.](/page/Washington,_D.C.) (July 9–11, 2024). These addressed alliance defense spending, hybrid threats, and transatlantic unity against [Russia](/page/Russia) and [China](/page/China). The 2021 Brussels agenda reaffirmed Article 5 and emerging challenges like cyber defense, with Biden declaring the alliance "stronger and more cohesive." [Madrid](/page/Madrid) adopted a new Strategic Concept naming [Russia](/page/Russia) as the primary threat and [China](/page/China) as a systemic challenge, alongside U.S.-led increases in [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) [military aid](/page/Military_aid). Vilnius advanced Ukraine's NATO integration path without membership action plan, committing to F-16 training and long-range weapons delivery. The 2024 Washington summit, marking NATO's 75th anniversary, secured over $40 billion in allied pledges for [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) security assistance, emphasizing burden-sharing with 23 members meeting 2% GDP defense spending targets.
Biden engaged in APEC leaders' meetings, including virtual participation in 2021, in-person attendance at the 2023 [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco) summit (November 15–17, hosted by the U.S.), and the 2024 [Lima](/page/Lima) meeting (November 15–16, [Peru](/page/Peru)). Discussions centered on trade facilitation, digital connectivity, and sustainable growth in the [Asia-Pacific](/page/Asia–Pacific). U.S. positions promoted open plurilateralism and [supply chain](/page/Supply_chain) diversification, with 2023 deliverables including the IPEF framework for resilient partnerships and commitments to ease trade costs by 2030.[[29]](#ref-29)
At [United Nations General Assembly](/page/United_Nations_General_Assembly) high-level weeks, Biden delivered addresses annually from 2021 to 2024 in New York, outlining U.S. [multilateralism](/page/Multilateralism) amid conflicts in [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) and the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East). Key positions included defending the UN Charter's rules-based order, urging cease-fires, and mobilizing for global challenges like pandemics and [climate](/page/Climate), though empirical outcomes showed limited consensus on enforcement mechanisms.[[30]](#ref-30)

### Outcomes of Key Fora

At the 2021 G7 Summit in [Carbis Bay](/page/Carbis_Bay), leaders launched the Build Back Better World (B3W) partnership to mobilize private capital for infrastructure in developing nations as an alternative to China's [Belt and Road Initiative](/page/Belt_and_Road_Initiative), though subsequent rebranding to the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment (PGII) in 2022 set a $600 billion mobilization target by 2027 with limited initial disbursements reported.[[31]](#ref-31)[[32]](#ref-32) The communique also committed to 1 billion [COVID-19 vaccine](/page/COVID-19_vaccine) doses for low-income countries by 2022, alongside pledges to end uneconomic international [coal](/page/Coal) financing.[[31]](#ref-31)
NATO's 2021 Brussels Summit endorsed plans for a new Strategic Concept, enhanced cyber defenses, and an action plan on [climate change](/page/Climate_change) and security, reaffirming collective defense under Article 5 while addressing emerging threats from [Russia](/page/Russia) and [China](/page/China).[[33]](#ref-33) At the 2022 Madrid Summit, Allies adopted the new Strategic Concept explicitly naming [Russia](/page/Russia) as the most significant direct threat and [China](/page/China) as a systemic challenge, invited [Finland](/page/Finland) and [Sweden](/page/Sweden) to join (with [Finland](/page/Finland) acceding in 2023), and committed to scaling high-readiness forces to over 300,000 troops.[[34]](#ref-34) The 2023 Vilnius Summit established the NATO-[Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) Council for equal-partner consultations, removed the Membership Action Plan requirement for [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine)'s accession, and pledged long-term security assistance without a timeline, signaling an "irreversible path" to membership when conditions are met.[[35]](#ref-35) The 2024 Washington Summit secured Allied commitments for at least €40 billion in security assistance to [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) over the following year, with 23 of 32 members meeting the 2% GDP defense spending guideline, and established a $1 billion NATO trust fund for [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine)'s defense industry.[[36]](#ref-36)[[37]](#ref-37)
G7 summits post-2022 invasion yielded quantifiable Ukraine support, including over $2.8 billion in humanitarian aid pledged at Elmau in 2022 and mechanisms at Hiroshima in 2023 to accelerate financial, military, and reconstruction assistance, such as using frozen Russian assets for recovery estimated at up to $300 billion.[[38]](#ref-38)[[39]](#ref-39) G20 declarations reflected enforcement challenges: the 2022 Bali outcome saw "most members" strongly condemn the war's human suffering without unanimous naming of Russia, while the 2023 New Delhi consensus called for a "comprehensive, just, and durable peace" via negotiation, omitting direct aggression attribution amid Global South divisions.[[40]](#ref-40)[[41]](#ref-41) These produced short-term alignments on sanctions and supply chain resilience but highlighted gaps in universal enforcement, with joint G7-NATO statements enabling coordinated asset freezes exceeding $300 billion globally.[[42]](#ref-42)

## Strategic Assessment

### Policy Achievements

Biden's international trips contributed to enhanced [NATO](/page/NATO) cohesion, evidenced by the accession of [Finland](/page/Finland) on April 4, 2023, and [Sweden](/page/Sweden) on [March 7](/page/March_7), 2024, expanding the [alliance](/page/Alliance) to 32 members and bolstering deterrence against Russian aggression following the 2022 [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) [invasion](/page/Invasion). These expansions followed U.S. [ratification](/page/Ratification) protocols signed by Biden on August 9, 2022, after multilateral engagements in [Europe](/page/Europe) that rallied allied support. [NATO](/page/NATO) defense spending surged, with all 32 allies projected to meet or exceed the 2% of GDP target in 2025, up from only three in 2014, reflecting commitments reinforced during summits attended by Biden. Collective [NATO](/page/NATO) defense expenditures reached approximately $1.6 trillion in 2025, a rise from $1.45 trillion in 2024, driven by European allies' increases post-[Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) crisis diplomacy.[[43]](#ref-43)[[44]](#ref-44)[[45]](#ref-45)
In the [Asia-Pacific](/page/Asia–Pacific), trips facilitated progress in trilateral and quadrilateral partnerships aimed at countering Chinese influence. The [AUKUS](/page/AUKUS) security pact, announced in September 2021, advanced under Biden with implementation of advanced capabilities, including submarine technology sharing, despite congressional hurdles. Quad Leaders' Summits, hosted or attended by Biden in 2022–2024, yielded initiatives like [maritime security](/page/Maritime_security) cooperation and infrastructure projects, with six leaders' meetings and eight foreign ministers' sessions enhancing regional deterrence. These engagements correlated with sustained allied military posture enhancements, including joint exercises and technology transfers.[[46]](#ref-46)[[47]](#ref-47)
The December 2024 trip to [Angola](/page/Angola) advanced the [Lobito](/page/Lobito) Corridor project, securing $600 million in U.S. commitments for rail upgrades spanning 1,344 km to access critical minerals like [cobalt](/page/Cobalt), fostering economic alternatives to Chinese dominance in African supply chains. This deal, involving U.S. loans up to $553 million for the [Lobito](/page/Lobito) Atlantic Railway, supported private investments and regional connectivity with [Zambia](/page/Zambia) and the [Democratic Republic](/page/Democratic_republic) of Congo. On climate fronts, trips aligned with U.S. fulfillment of $11 billion annual international financing pledges by 2024, though measurable emission reductions remain tied to domestic policies rather than direct trip outcomes.[[48]](#ref-48)[[49]](#ref-49)[[50]](#ref-50)

### Criticisms and Shortcomings

Critics have argued that Biden's international trips exhibited a reactive posture, with an overemphasis on [Europe](/page/Europe) amid escalating challenges from [China](/page/China) in the [Indo-Pacific](/page/Indo-Pacific) and beyond. Through 2023, approximately 40% of Biden's foreign visits focused on European allies, including multiple [NATO](/page/NATO) summits and bilateral engagements, while direct travel to [Asia](/page/Asia) totaled fewer than ten instances, allowing [Beijing](/page/Beijing) to expand economic and diplomatic influence unchecked in regions like [Southeast Asia](/page/Southeast_Asia).[[51]](#ref-51) This Europe-centric approach, per analyses from strategic observers, diverted resources from countering China's Belt and Road initiatives, which secured over $1 trillion in global infrastructure deals by 2023, often in areas underserved by U.S. presence.[[52]](#ref-52)
Engagement with adversaries remained limited post-2021, contributing to empirical shortfalls in deterrence. The June 2021 Geneva summit with [Vladimir Putin](/page/Vladimir_Putin) yielded no verifiable [de-escalation](/page/De-escalation), as [Russia](/page/Russia) proceeded with its full-scale [invasion](/page/Invasion) of [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) eight months later, underscoring a failure to alter Moscow's calculus despite U.S. warnings.[[53]](#ref-53) Similarly, in-person meetings with Chinese President [Xi Jinping](/page/Xi_Jinping) were rare—limited to one multilateral sideline encounter in [Bali](/page/Bali) in November 2022—amid rising tensions over [Taiwan](/page/Taiwan) and trade, with no subsequent bilateral summits altering Beijing's assertive posture in the [South China Sea](/page/South_China_Sea).[[54]](#ref-54) Think tank assessments, including from the [American Enterprise Institute](/page/American_Enterprise_Institute), attribute these outcomes to perceived U.S. signaling weakness, contrasting with defenses emphasizing alliance consultations that, while unifying [NATO](/page/NATO) on sanctions, did not prevent post-trip escalations like [Russia](/page/Russia)'s territorial gains in [Donbas](/page/Donbas).[[53]](#ref-53)
Regional neglect in [Africa](/page/Africa) and [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) exacerbated opportunity costs, enabling Chinese inroads until belated 2024 visits. Biden conducted no standalone state visits to [sub-Saharan Africa](/page/Sub-Saharan_Africa) until December 2024's [Angola](/page/Angola) trip, during which [China](/page/China) had already invested over $300 billion continent-wide since 2000, securing [mining](/page/Mining) rights and ports that advanced its resource security.[[55]](#ref-55) In [Latin America](/page/Latin_America), trips were confined largely to multilateral forums, totaling just two more than Trump's tally by term's end, as [Beijing](/page/Beijing) expanded trade ties—reaching $450 billion annually by 2023—filling voids in infrastructure where U.S. commitments lagged.[[56]](#ref-56) [Heritage Foundation](/page/The_Heritage_Foundation) critiques highlight how this deferred focus undermined deterrence against authoritarian influence, prioritizing reactive [Europe](/page/Europe) responses over proactive hemispheric engagement.[[57]](#ref-57)
High operational costs juxtaposed against domestic priorities drew scrutiny, with federal expenditures on presidential travel exceeding $100 million annually by fiscal year 2022, per Government Accountability Office audits, amid stalled U.S. infrastructure reforms.[[58]](#ref-58) Optics issues compounded perceptions of inefficacy, including gaffes at [NATO](/page/NATO) summits—such as misnaming allies—and questions over physical stamina during extended itineraries, with Biden citing [jet lag](/page/Jet_lag) from prior trips as a factor in unrelated performance lapses, fueling narratives of diminished projection of strength.[[59]](#ref-59)[[60]](#ref-60) While administration officials countered that trips bolstered deterrence through multilateral unity, verifiable metrics like persistent Russian advances and Chinese economic dependencies reveal unmitigated strategic dependencies.[[61]](#ref-61)

The international presidential trips made by [Joe Biden](/page/Joe_Biden) comprise his 36 official foreign visits as the 46th [President of the United States](/page/President_of_the_United_States), spanning January 20, 2021, to January 20, 2025, to 27 countries across [Europe](/page/Europe), [Asia](/page/Asia), the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East), [Africa](/page/Africa), and the [Americas](/page/Americas).[[1]](#ref-1) These travels emphasized multilateral diplomacy, including attendance at seven [G7](/page/G7) summits, five [G20](/page/G20) summits, and five [NATO](/page/NATO) summits, alongside bilateral engagements to coordinate responses to Russia's 2022 invasion of [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) and strategic competition with [China](/page/China) in the [Indo-Pacific](/page/Indo-Pacific).[[1]](#ref-1)
Biden's itinerary reflected a pattern of frequent European visits—13 in total—to reinforce NATO cohesion and deliver security assistance commitments, such as during his historic wartime trip to [Kyiv](/page/Kyiv) in February 2023, the first by a sitting U.S. president since the early [2000s](/page/2000s).[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2) In [Asia](/page/Asia), nine trips advanced partnerships through forums like the Quad and U.S.-[ASEAN](/page/ASEAN) summits, including state visits to [Japan](/page/Japan), [South Korea](/page/South_Korea), and [Vietnam](/page/Vietnam) to elevate economic and defense ties.[[1]](#ref-1) Later journeys marked precedents, such as the first presidential visits to [Angola](/page/Angola) in December 2024 and delayed engagements in [South America](/page/South_America) ([Peru](/page/Peru) and [Brazil](/page/Brazil) in November 2024), amid criticisms of delayed focus on regions like [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) and sub-[Saharan Africa](/page/Sub-Saharan_Africa) relative to predecessors.[[1]](#ref-1)[[3]](#ref-3) Early travel was constrained by the [COVID-19 pandemic](/page/COVID-19_pandemic), resulting in only six international trips in 2021—all to [Europe](/page/Europe)—compared to higher volumes by prior administrations in their initial years, before accelerating to 12 in 2022.[[4]](#ref-4) Defining elements included climate-focused attendance at COP26 and regional security consultations, such as in the Gulf and with Nordic leaders, though outcomes faced scrutiny over alliance strains and limited tangible concessions from adversaries like [Russia](/page/Russia) and [China](/page/China).[[1]](#ref-1)

## Summary

### Total Trips and Destinations

President Joe Biden conducted 21 international trips during his term, visiting 28 [countries](/page/List_of_companies_and_cities_in_Africa_that_manufacture_cement) in total, as documented in official records of presidential travels.[[1]](#ref-1) These engagements spanned [Europe](/page/Europe) (12 [countries](/page/List_of_companies_and_cities_in_Africa_that_manufacture_cement), including multiple returns to the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom), [Germany](/page/Germany), and [Poland](/page/Poland)), [Asia](/page/Asia) (9 [countries](/page/List_of_companies_and_cities_in_Africa_that_manufacture_cement), such as [Japan](/page/Japan), [India](/page/India), and [Vietnam](/page/Vietnam)), the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East) ([Israel](/page/Israel), [Saudi Arabia](/page/Saudi_Arabia), and the [West Bank](/page/West_Bank)), [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) ([Mexico](/page/Mexico), [Peru](/page/Peru), and [Brazil](/page/Brazil)), and [Africa](/page/Africa) ([Angola](/page/Angola) and [Cape Verde](/page/Cape_Verde)). The distribution emphasized [Europe](/page/Europe), accounting for the majority of destinations, with lighter representation from [Africa](/page/Africa) and [Latin America](/page/Latin_America) until the final year of his presidency.
Biden's travel included first-ever presidential visits to [Angola](/page/Angola) and [Cape Verde](/page/Cape_Verde) in December 2024, the latter part of a single African itinerary focused on sub-Saharan engagement after previous postponements of similar plans.[[5]](#ref-5)[[2]](#ref-2) Other delays affected destinations like an earlier [Angola](/page/Angola) trip and a [Germany](/page/Germany) visit, which occurred in October 2024.[[6]](#ref-6)
In comparison to predecessors, Biden's early-term pace—two trips in 2021, primarily to [Europe](/page/Europe)—was more restrained than Barack Obama's 13 trips in his first year or George W. Bush's 10, reflecting initial priorities on domestic [pandemic](/page/Pandemic) recovery and limited global mobility.[[7]](#ref-7) By contrast, [Donald](/page/Donald) Trump's first-year total reached 5 trips. Travel accelerated in 2022 with 7 itineraries across [Europe](/page/Europe), [Asia](/page/Asia), and the [Middle East](/page/Middle_East), aligning closer to historical norms for second-year engagements.[[4]](#ref-4)

### Primary Objectives and Patterns

The primary objectives of Joe Biden's international trips, as articulated in [White House](/page/White_House) statements, centered on restoring U.S. leadership among democracies, coordinating with [NATO](/page/NATO) allies on security challenges, and countering strategic competitors like [China](/page/China) through Indo-Pacific partnerships.[[8]](#ref-8)[[9]](#ref-9) Early rationales emphasized multilateral alliance reinforcement to address post-Afghanistan credibility concerns and global issues such as climate cooperation, reflecting a causal priority on rebuilding transatlantic unity amid perceived prior [isolationism](/page/Isolationism).[[10]](#ref-10)
Geopolitical patterns reveal a pronounced clustering of trips in [Europe](/page/Europe), driven by reactive responses to Russian threats, including the 2022 Ukraine invasion, which necessitated repeated [NATO](/page/NATO) and bilateral ally consultations for deterrence and support coordination.[[4]](#ref-4) This [Europe](/page/Europe)-centric focus—accounting for eight visits—contrasted with sparser [Asia](/page/Asia) engagements aimed at [China](/page/China) containment via alliances like the Quad, underscoring causal drivers of crisis proximity over balanced global outreach.[[6]](#ref-6) Travel frequency peaked early in the term with six international trips in 2021, declining markedly in 2024 to seven amid domestic election demands, a pattern attributable to resource allocation toward U.S. political imperatives rather than sustained foreign [diplomacy](/page/Diplomacy).[[4]](#ref-4)[[2]](#ref-2)
Over time, trip rationales shifted from broad multilateral resets in 2021—such as [G7](/page/G7) and [NATO](/page/NATO) summits—to more granular bilateral pledges, particularly for [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) aid and targeted [Asia](/page/Asia) diplomacy against [China](/page/China) expansionism, evidencing an evolution from foundational alliance repair to operational crisis management.[[11]](#ref-11) Logistically, these engagements relied on [Air Force One](/page/Air_Force_One) for secure transit, with per-hour operational costs exceeding $177,000, amplifying the fiscal stakes of such patterned deployments.[[12]](#ref-12) This progression highlights underlying causal realism: initial proactive multilateralism yielded to reactive [bilateralism](/page/Bilateralism) as acute threats like Russian aggression demanded direct, alliance-specific interventions over generalized forums.[[13]](#ref-13)

## Chronological Trips

### 2021 Trips

President Joe Biden's international travel in 2021 consisted of two multi-country trips to Europe, marking his initial efforts to engage with allies following his January inauguration and amid the U.S. military drawdown in Afghanistan. These visits emphasized multilateral summits to reaffirm transatlantic partnerships strained under prior administrations.[[1]](#ref-1)
The first trip spanned June 9 to 16, beginning in the [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom) at [Cornwall](/page/Cornwall) for the [G7](/page/G7) Summit, where Biden met Prime Minister [Boris Johnson](/page/Boris_Johnson) and Queen Elizabeth II.[[1]](#ref-1) He then proceeded to [Brussels](/page/Brussels), [Belgium](/page/Belgium), from June 13 to 15, meeting King Philippe and Prime Minister [Alexander De Croo](/page/Alexander_De_Croo) while attending the [NATO Summit](/page/NATO_summit).[[1]](#ref-1) The itinerary concluded in [Geneva](/page/Geneva), [Switzerland](/page/Switzerland), on June 15 to 16, involving meetings with President [Guy Parmelin](/page/Guy_Parmelin) and Foreign Minister [Ignazio Cassis](/page/Ignazio_Cassis), followed by a bilateral summit with Russian President [Vladimir Putin](/page/Vladimir_Putin).[[1]](#ref-1)

### 2022 Trips

In 2022, President Biden's international travel intensified in response to Russia's invasion of [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) on February 24, prioritizing coordination with [NATO](/page/NATO) allies and [European](/page/Europe) partners through emergency summits and bilateral visits. This marked a pivot toward [Europe](/page/Europe), with five trips to the continent in the first half of the year, including attendance at an extraordinary [NATO summit](/page/NATO_summit) in [Brussels](/page/Brussels) on March 24–25 and a subsequent visit to [Warsaw](/page/Warsaw), [Poland](/page/Poland), on March 25–26, where he met President [Andrzej Duda](/page/Andrzej_Duda) and inspected U.S. aid shipments at Rzeszów-Jasionka Airport, a key logistics hub for [Ukraine](/page/Ukraine) support. These engagements underscored immediate crisis response, contrasting with fewer pre-invasion travels.[[1]](#ref-1)

## Multilateral Engagements

### Major Summits Attended

Biden engaged in APEC leaders' meetings, including virtual participation in 2021, in-person attendance at the 2023 [San Francisco](/page/San_Francisco) summit (November 15–17, hosted by the U.S.), and the 2024 [Lima](/page/Lima) meeting (November 15–16, [Peru](/page/Peru)).
